standard.title: Multiply and divide by powers of 10
standard.description: Solve problems involving multiplying or dividing natural numbers by multiples and powers of 10 without a calculator, using the multiplicative relationship between the place value of digits
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can recognise and represent numbers beyond 10 000 and understand place value conventions (AC9M3N01); they can multiply and divide one- and two-digit numbers (AC9M3N04). They have not yet applied the multiplicative structure of place value to multiply or divide by 10, 100 or 1000.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students solve problems involving multiplying and dividing natural numbers by multiples and powers of 10 by applying the multiplicative relationship between place value positions.

nodes.label: Multiplying by 10 — digit movement
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain and demonstrate that multiplying by 10 moves each digit one place to the left.
nodes.minimum_width: Use materials or a place value chart to show that 34 × 10 = 340; explain why each digit moves one place to the left.
nodes.typical_width: Use place value charts, numeral expanders or sliders to demonstrate multiplying by 10 across multiple examples; explain why digits move left (each place becomes ten times larger); generalise the pattern.
wider: Use numeral expanders or sliders to make visible the digit movement interpretation — physically sliding digits left and discussing whether 'adding a zero' captures the same idea or misrepresents it
Connect multiplication by 10 to metric unit conversions (e.g. 3 m × 10 = 30 dm or 3.0 m = 30 dm) — applying the pattern to measurement

response_modes.reason: Common misconception: 'multiply by 10 means add a zero.' This works for whole numbers but breaks down for decimals (0.3 × 10 ≠ 0.30). The correct conceptual model — digits move left — is the hinge. Seeing the pattern in place value charts, sliders and measurement contexts prevents the 'add a zero' shortcut from calcifying.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who hold the 'add a zero' model enter Node 2 with a rule that fails for ×100 and ×1000 edge cases and entirely for decimals. The digit-movement model is the prerequisite conceptual frame for generalising to all powers of 10.
success_criteria: Students can multiply a two- or three-digit number by 10 without a calculator and explain the digit movement
Students can explain why the rule works using place value language (not just 'add a zero')

nodes.label: Dividing by 10 and extending to 100 and 1000
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can multiply and divide by 10, 100 and 1000 using the place value relationship, and solve related problems.
nodes.minimum_width: Divide one number by 10 using a place value chart and explain the digit movement; solve one multiplication problem involving 100.
nodes.typical_width: Use place value charts to demonstrate multiplication and division by 10, 100 and 1000; generalise the pattern (number of places = number of zeros); apply to solve computation problems without a calculator; use digital tools to check and extend the pattern.
wider: Investigate the pattern using a spreadsheet: enter numbers and apply ×10, ×100, ×1000 formulas, record results in a place value table and generalise the pattern from 100 terms
Apply the place value pattern to multi-step problems involving metric conversions (e.g. how many millimetres in 4.5 metres?)

response_modes.reason: Students need to build a repertoire of related problems they can solve using this rule — not just ×10 but ×100, ÷10, ÷100, and related combinations. A narrow exposure to ×10 alone leaves gaps when ×100 and ×1000 appear.

success_criteria: Students can multiply and divide a number by 10, 100 and 1000 without a calculator
Students can solve a practical problem by identifying that ×10 or ÷10 is needed and applying it correctly
